title: Israel from the exodus to Solomon
premise: The Bible gives the years from the exodus to Solomon as a run of numbers and a string of places. The ground gives sites, layers and ranges of dates. This study sets the two side by side, from the stay in Egypt to Solomon's gates, and shows exactly where the evidence and the text meet. It also shows where scholars join them in different ways, and where the ground has nothing to say.
question: When a date for these events is offered, is it a number the text gives, a range the ground gives, or a scholar's way of joining the two?
outcomes: Name the three numbers in Scripture that every exodus date rests on (1 Kings 6:1, Exodus 12:40, Judges 11:26), and say how each of the two main dates reads them.
Tell the two readings of the 430 years in Exodus 12:40 apart, and say which ancient texts and which Jewish and Christian readers stand behind each.
For Jericho, Ai, Hazor and Shiloh, say what was found, when the excavators date it, and what the find can and cannot show about Joshua and the judges.
Explain why one six-chambered gate can be dated to Solomon by one archaeologist and to a later king by another, and what radiocarbon has and has not settled.
Describe fairly the view that Israel's early history was invented, in its holders' terms, and give the evidence its critics answer with.

boundaries.in: Israel's history from the stay in Egypt to the death of Solomon, read beside the ground and the outside records: the length of the stay, the date of the exodus, the entry into the land at Ai and Hazor, the highland villages, Shiloh, Saul's and David's years with Khirbet Qeiyafa and Jerusalem's stepped stone structure, and Solomon's gates at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer with the debate over the tenth century BC.
out: Jericho's layers in detail: Cities through their layers (08) reads them. Here its dates are cited, with Kenyon and Wood side by side.
The Merneptah stele and the Tel Dan stele as objects: Archaeology and the Bible (06) reads them. Here each is cited for what it fixes.
The Habiru of the Amarna letters: The Bible and the ancient Near East (32) counts the word. Here the question of whether any Hebrews were called Habiru is named and left with both views.
Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Joseph's rise: The patriarchs in their world (39). This study begins where Jacob's family is already in Egypt.
The method of reckoning kings' reigns, and the year of Solomon's fourth year: Old Testament chronology (10). This study uses that study's rounded date and says so.
The kings after Solomon and Shoshenq's campaign as a whole: Israel among the empires (07).
Who wrote the books of Moses, Joshua, Judges, Samuel and Kings, and when: How the Old Testament books were written.
The tabernacle and Solomon's temple as places of worship: The temple and Israel's worship.
What these events mean for faith: the theology studies Moses, David, The kings of Israel and Judah and Scripture (the word of God).

stationsLead: Six stations, in the Bible's own order. Each gives the passage, what the ground or an outside record says, what this study infers, and where the evidence stops. No station needs an exodus date to be read, and none chooses one.

stations.name: The stay in Egypt
stations.headline: Four hundred and thirty years. Counted from where?
stations.lead: Exodus 12:40 gives the length of Israel's stay as 430 years, and Exodus 12:41 says the LORD's hosts went out at the end of them, to the day. Genesis 15:13 gives Abraham a rounded 400 years of affliction in a land not his own. Paul, in Galatians 3:17, puts the law 430 years after the promise. The question is not whether the numbers are true. It is what they count.

records.title: The verse in three ancient forms
records.evidence: The Hebrew (Masoretic) text of Exodus 12:40 counts the 430 years for the time the Israelites lived in Egypt. The Greek translation (the Septuagint) and the Samaritan Pentateuch read, in substance, that they lived in Egypt and in the land of Canaan for 430 years, so that the patriarchs' years in Canaan are counted in.
records.inference: Two ways of reading the verse are therefore older than any modern scholar. One gives about 430 years in Egypt; the other gives about 215, with the other 215 running from Abraham's arrival in Canaan to Jacob's going down to Egypt.
records.limit: The ancient forms show that the question was asked early. They do not settle which reading the writer of Exodus meant. The Berean follows the Hebrew text in its main line [check: whether the Berean prints a footnote at Exodus 12:40 giving the Greek and Samaritan reading, and its exact wording].

records.title: The Jewish reading first
records.evidence: The rabbinic chronology Seder Olam Rabbah counts the 430 years from God's covenant with Abraham, and gives the time in Egypt as 210 years. Rashi, the medieval Jewish commentator, explains Exodus 12:40 the same way, counting from the covenant between the pieces in Genesis 15 [check: Rashi's exact starting point at Exodus 12:40, the covenant or Isaac's birth, and the Seder Olam chapter]. Josephus, the first-century Jewish historian, also gives 215 years in Egypt [check: Antiquities 2.15.2, section 318].
records.inference: The shorter stay is not a modern harmonisation. It is how a large part of Jewish tradition has read the verse, and Paul's count in Galatians 3:17 runs from the promise, as theirs does.
records.limit: Paul's purpose in Galatians is to set the law after the promise, not to give a chronology of Egypt. Readers on both sides of this question cite him.

records.title: Four generations, or more
records.evidence: Exodus 6:16–20 runs Levi, Kohath, Amram and Moses, and gives the ages of the first three at death. Genesis 15:16 says Abraham's descendants would return in the fourth generation.
records.inference: Readers of the short stay find four generations easier to fit into about 215 years. Readers of the long stay answer that Hebrew genealogies often skip generations, so the list names the line, not every link in it. Kitchen argues this from other ancient Near Eastern lists [check: page in On the Reliability of the Old Testament].
records.limit: Neither reading needs the genealogy to be wrong. They differ on whether it is complete.

records.title: Semites in the eastern Delta
records.evidence: Excavations at Tell el-Dab'a, ancient Avaris, in the eastern Nile Delta, led by Manfred Bietak, show a large population of West Semitic origin there in the Middle Bronze Age, before and during the rule of the Hyksos kings. A tomb painting at Beni Hasan, from the time of the official Khnumhotep II (about 1890 BC, as usually dated [check]), shows a party of Asiatics arriving in Egypt. A papyrus in the Brooklyn Museum (35.1446) lists household servants, many with Semitic names [check: the names Hoffmeier cites from it].
records.inference: Semitic people living and working in the Delta is well attested for the centuries in which both readings place Jacob's family. The setting fits the story.
records.limit: None of these finds names Jacob, Joseph or Israel. A setting that fits is not a record of the event. Who the Semites at Avaris were is argued, and this study does not identify them with Israel.

records.title: Pithom and Raamses
records.evidence: Exodus 1:11 names the store cities Pithom and Raamses. The great Delta capital Pi-Ramesses, at modern Qantir beside Tell el-Dab'a, was built under Rameses II in the 13th century BC. Genesis 47:11 already calls the land Jacob's family received the land of Rameses.
records.inference: Readers of the late exodus date take Raamses as the name of the city in the time of the oppression, and so a pointer to the 13th century. Readers of the early date answer that Genesis 47:11 uses the name for Joseph's day too, so the name may be the later one by which readers knew the place, set into the account.
records.limit: The name alone cannot decide the date: both readings account for it. Where Pithom stood is itself argued (Tell el-Maskhuta and Tell er-Retabeh are both proposed [check: who holds each]).

stations.name: The exodus and its date
stations.headline: Four hundred and eighty years. A count or a measure?
stations.lead: 1 Kings 6:1 dates the start of Solomon's temple to the 480th year after Israel came out of Egypt, in the fourth year of his reign. Old Testament chronology (10) puts that fourth year at about 966 BC, by the usual reckoning. Everything turns on what the 480 years are.

records.title: Read as a count: about 1446 BC
records.evidence: Adding 480 years to about 966 BC gives about 1446 BC. In Judges 11:26 Jephthah tells the king of Ammon that Israel has held the land east of the Jordan for 300 years.
records.inference: Bryant Wood and Eugene Merrill take the 480 years as a count of years, which places the exodus in Egypt's 18th dynasty, with Thutmose III or Amenhotep II as the pharaoh, and Jephthah's 300 years as agreeing with it. Merrill sets this out in Kingdom of Priests [check: edition and chapter].
records.limit: No Egyptian record of the 18th dynasty names Israel or the plagues. The early date rests on the text's numbers, read as counts, and on a reading of sites such as Jericho, Ai and Hazor that its holders argue for site by site.

records.title: Read as a measure: about 1260 BC
records.evidence: Exodus 1:11 names Raamses. Highland villages multiply in the 12th century BC. The Merneptah stele, about 1208 BC, names Israel as a people in Canaan (cited from Archaeology and the Bible, 06).
records.inference: Kenneth Kitchen and James Hoffmeier hold a date in the 13th century BC, under Rameses II, around 1260 BC [check: the decade each gives]. They read the 480 years as twelve generations, each given a conventional forty years, or as a total that can be checked against the spans of Judges added differently. Kitchen argues this in On the Reliability of the Old Testament; Hoffmeier in Israel in Egypt and Ancient Israel in Sinai.
records.limit: The late date also has no Egyptian record of the exodus itself. It rests on a reading of 1 Kings 6:1 that its critics think strains the plain sense, and it must explain Jephthah's 300 years.

records.title: What both sides share
records.evidence: Wood, Merrill, Kitchen and Hoffmeier all hold that the exodus happened as Scripture says. They differ on how its numbers are meant to be read and on how the ground is dated.
records.inference: This is a disagreement inside belief in Scripture's truth. It is not a choice between believing and doubting the text.
records.limit: This study does not choose between them. The Baptist Faith and Message 2000 affirms Scripture as truth without any mixture of error and names no date.

records.title: An earlier Israel on a pedestal?
records.evidence: In 2012 Manfred Görg, Peter van der Veen and Christoffer Theis proposed that a broken name ring on a statue pedestal in Berlin (Ägyptisches Museum 21687) reads Israel, and dates to the 18th dynasty [check: the inventory number and the year of publication].
records.inference: If the reading holds, Israel was known to Egypt earlier than the Merneptah stele, which some early-date readers count in their favour.
records.limit: The reading of the name is disputed, and the date of the pedestal's list is argued. It is reported here as a proposal, not a finding.

records.title: How many came out
records.evidence: Exodus 12:37 gives about 600,000 men on foot, besides children.
records.inference: Most readers take the number at its face. Some evangelical scholars, among them Colin Humphreys and others, have argued that the Hebrew word usually rendered thousand can mean a clan unit, which would give a smaller total [check: the holders and their works before naming them on the page].
records.limit: This is a question of a word's meaning, not of the ground. The desert leaves little trace of people who lived in tents, so the ground cannot count them.

stations.name: Entering the land
stations.headline: Three cities burned, says Joshua. Which layers burned, says the ground.
stations.lead: Joshua names only three cities as burned: Jericho, Ai and Hazor. The rest of the land is taken, Joshua 11:13 says, without its cities on their mounds being burned. So the ground is asked a narrow question: what burned at these three, and when?

records.title: Jericho, cited
records.evidence: Kathleen Kenyon, excavating from 1952 to 1958, dated the city's last great destruction to the end of the Middle Bronze Age, about 1550 BC, and found little of the Late Bronze Age above it. Bryant Wood, re-examining the pottery from John Garstang's and Kenyon's work in 1990, dated the same destruction to about 1400 BC [check: Biblical Archaeology Review 16:2 (1990)]. Radiocarbon dates published by Hendrik Bruins and Johannes van der Plicht in 1995 favour the earlier date [check: the journal and the range given].
records.inference: Kenyon's date leaves no walled city for a late-date Joshua and none for an early-date Joshua either. Wood's date fits the early exodus. Late-date readers answer that Late Bronze Jericho has largely eroded away.
records.limit: Cities through their layers (08) reads the layers themselves; this page cites the two dates only. Both rest on pottery and samples from a mound that had already been heavily dug.

records.title: Ai: where did it stand?
records.evidence: Et-Tell, east of Bethel, is the site most scholars identify as Ai. Judith Marquet-Krause (1933–1935) and Joseph Callaway (1964–1972) found a large Early Bronze Age city, abandoned many centuries before either exodus date, and a small village of the early Iron Age, but no occupation in the Late Bronze Age [check: the end date of the Early Bronze city]. Callaway taught at the Southern Baptist Theological Seminary. Bryant Wood argues that Ai stood at Khirbet el-Maqatir, about a kilometre west of et-Tell, where excavations by the Associates for Biblical Research under Wood (from 1995) and later Scott Stripling found a small fortress of the Late Bronze Age with signs of destruction by fire [check: the excavation seasons and the published dating].
records.inference: If Ai is et-Tell, the ground shows no city at the time of either exodus date, and readers have proposed that the story's Ai was a ruin used as a stronghold, or that the name refers to the nearby village. If Ai is Khirbet el-Maqatir, there is a fortress of the right age. William Albright suggested an older answer, that the Ai story preserved a memory of Bethel's fall [check: Albright's work]; David Livingston argued for a different site for Bethel altogether, which moves Ai with it [check].
records.limit: The placement of Ai depends on where Bethel was and on reading the geography of Joshua 7–8. The ground at each site is real; which site the text means is a judgment. This study shows both and does not choose.

records.title: Hazor's great fire
records.evidence: Yigael Yadin (1955–1958, 1968) and Amnon Ben-Tor (from 1990) found that Hazor, the largest city in Canaan, ended in the 13th century BC in a severe fire, with statues of gods and kings deliberately damaged [check: the dating range Ben-Tor gives].
records.inference: Ben-Tor connects this destruction with Israel, in keeping with Joshua 11. Sharon Zuckerman has argued instead for a revolt within the city [check: her publication]. Late-date readers see Joshua's burning here. Early-date readers, among them Wood, argue for an earlier destruction around 1400 BC as Joshua's and take the 13th-century fire as the defeat of Jabin in Judges 4 [check: Wood's publication and whether he holds both parts of this].
records.limit: The ground shows who suffered the fire, not who set it. No inscription from the destruction names an attacker.

records.title: The Habiru, cited
records.evidence: The Amarna letters of the 14th century BC complain of armed bands called Habiru. The Bible and the ancient Near East (32) counts the word and shows that it is used along the whole coast.
records.inference: Some early-date readers have connected the Habiru with Joshua's Israel; most scholars take the word as a name for a kind of person rather than a nation.
records.limit: The letters name no Israel and no Joshua. This study leaves the question open, as 32 does.

stations.name: The highland villages and the judges
stations.headline: Hundreds of small villages. One name on a stone.
stations.lead: Judges describes a people living in the hill country, unable at first to drive the Canaanites out of the valleys and the coast (Judges 1:27–35). In the early Iron Age, from about 1200 BC, the central hill country fills with small villages where few had stood before.

records.title: The surveys
records.evidence: Surveys of the central hill country, among them Israel Finkelstein's and Adam Zertal's, counted a sharp rise in small, unwalled villages in Iron Age I, from a few dozen sites in the Late Bronze Age to some hundreds [check: the figures given in Finkelstein, The Archaeology of the Israelite Settlement (1988)]. The villages share a house plan with four spaces (the four-room house), large storage jars with a raised rim at the neck (collared-rim jars), terraces and cisterns, and in many cases few or no pig bones.
records.inference: Most archaeologists identify many of these villagers with the people the Merneptah stele calls Israel. That they lived in the hills, in small farming groups, matches the picture in Judges.
records.limit: Pots and houses do not carry names. The same house and jar are found outside the hills, and the lack of pig bones has other possible explanations, as Brian Hesse and Paula Wapnish cautioned [check: their article]. Where the villagers came from is argued: from outside, from Canaan's own lowlands, or from settling herders. The text says Israel entered from outside; this study reports the ground's ambiguity and leaves the reading of it to each holder.

records.title: Merneptah, cited
records.evidence: On the stele of Merneptah, about 1208 BC, Israel appears among peoples and towns Pharaoh claims to have defeated in Canaan, written with the sign Egyptian scribes used for a people rather than a city. Archaeology and the Bible (06) reads the stone.
records.inference: Israel was a people in Canaan, known to Egypt, by about 1208 BC. Both exodus dates accept this: late-date readers place Israel's arrival a generation or so earlier, early-date readers about two centuries earlier.
records.limit: The stele fixes a latest date for Israel's presence in Canaan. It says nothing of how or when Israel arrived.

records.title: Mount Ebal
records.evidence: Adam Zertal excavated a structure on Mount Ebal in the 1980s, dated to the early Iron Age, with burnt animal bones around it [check: dates of excavation and the bones identified].
records.inference: Zertal identified it as the altar of Joshua 8:30–31. Others, among them Aharon Kempinski, read it as a watchtower or a farmstead [check: Kempinski's reply].
records.limit: The structure is real and early. Whether it is an altar, and whether it is Joshua's, is interpretation.

records.title: Shiloh
records.evidence: Shiloh is excavated at Khirbet Seilun, north of Bethel, matching the directions in Judges 21:19. Danish excavations (1920s–1930s), Israel Finkelstein (1981–1984) and, from 2017, the Associates for Biblical Research under Scott Stripling dug there. Finkelstein found an Iron Age I site with pillared storage buildings, destroyed by fire, which he dated to the middle of the 11th century BC [check: Finkelstein's dating and publication].
records.inference: Many readers connect the burning with the Philistine victory of 1 Samuel 4, which Psalm 78:60 and Jeremiah 7:12 remember as God forsaking Shiloh. Samuel does not say Shiloh was burned; the psalm and Jeremiah imply its ruin.
records.limit: No building has been identified beyond argument as the tabernacle's site, though proposals have been made. The fire's attacker is not named on the ground.

records.title: The years of the judges
records.evidence: Added end to end, the periods given in Judges come to well over 400 years [check: the exact sum as usually given].
records.inference: Early-date and late-date readers alike take several judges as ruling at the same time in different regions, since Judges itself places them in different tribes. Late-date readers must overlap them more.
records.limit: The book does not give a combined total, so any overlap is a reconstruction. Old Testament chronology (10) shows the reckonings.

stations.name: Saul and David
stations.headline: A fortress in the valley of Elah. A name on a stone in Dan.
stations.lead: Samuel tells of Saul's struggle with the Philistines, David's fight in the valley of Elah, and David's taking of the stronghold of Zion. The tenth century BC, where both exodus dates place David, is the hardest century in the land to date precisely.

records.title: Saul's Gibeah
records.evidence: William Albright excavated Tell el-Ful, north of Jerusalem, in the 1920s and 1930s and identified a fortress there with Saul's Gibeah; Paul Lapp dug again in 1964 [check: dates and the strata assigned].
records.inference: If the identification and dating hold, it is Saul's seat. Later scholars have questioned both the fortress's date and the identification [check: who].
records.limit: No inscription names the site. Saul's kingdom, as Samuel describes it, was small and centred on Benjamin, and would leave little building.

records.title: Khirbet Qeiyafa
records.evidence: Yosef Garfinkel and Saar Ganor excavated Khirbet Qeiyafa above the valley of Elah from 2007 to 2013. They found a single-period fortified town with a wall of double construction (a casemate wall) and two gates, dated by radiocarbon on olive pits to about the late 11th or early 10th century BC [check: the range published]. A potsherd with five lines of ink writing (an ostracon) was found in 2008. No pig bones were found.
records.inference: Garfinkel connects the town with David's kingdom and with Shaaraim, a name meaning two gates, which appears in Joshua 15:36 and 1 Samuel 17:52. Israel Finkelstein and Alexander Fantalkin have argued it could belong to an early northern or Benjaminite polity, perhaps in Saul's day, rather than Judah [check: their article]. Gershon Galil read the ostracon as Hebrew; Christopher Rollston and others hold that its language cannot yet be fixed [check: their publications].
records.limit: The town is well dated and planned, and it shows organised building in the Judean lowland at about the time Samuel places Saul and David. The ground does not say whose town it was.

records.title: Jerusalem's stepped stone structure
records.evidence: On the eastern slope of the City of David, a great mantle of stones climbs the hill. Kathleen Kenyon and then Yigal Shiloh (1978–1985) excavated it. In 2005 Eilat Mazar uncovered a large building on the summit above it, which she called the Large Stone Structure.
records.inference: Eilat Mazar identified the building as David's palace, built after 2 Samuel 5:11, with the stepped stone structure as part of the same work. Jane Cahill and Amihai Mazar date the stepped structure to the late 12th to 10th centuries BC [check: their ranges]. Israel Finkelstein and others date parts of the summit building later, some to well after Solomon [check: the publication].
records.limit: The stones are on the summit Scripture names. Their dates come from pottery in fills that were moved and rebuilt over centuries, and no inscription names a king. Some readers connect the stepped structure with the Millo of 2 Samuel 5:9; this is a proposal.

records.title: Tel Dan, cited
records.evidence: A broken stele from Tel Dan, of the 9th century BC, mentions a king of the house of David. Archaeology and the Bible (06) reads it.
records.inference: Within about a century and a half of David's reign, a foreign king knew Judah's royal line by David's name.
records.limit: The stele is later than David and tells nothing of his own reign. That the phrase reads house of David is accepted by most scholars, and The peoples around Israel (35) shows the readings.

stations.name: Solomon and the tenth century
stations.headline: One verse names three gates. The ground has three gates. When were they built?
stations.lead: 1 Kings 9:15 lists Solomon's forced labour for building the LORD's house, his own house, the Millo, Jerusalem's wall, and Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer. At all three cities archaeologists found gates of the same plan, with six chambers. The debate over the tenth century BC is whether they are Solomon's.

records.title: Three gates of one plan
records.evidence: Yigael Yadin found a six-chambered gate at Hazor and saw the same plan in the gate at Megiddo excavated earlier. In 1958 he identified a similar gate at Gezer in R. A. S. Macalister's old plans, where Macalister had called the wall a Maccabean castle [check: Israel Exploration Journal 8 (1958)]. William Dever's excavations at Gezer from the 1960s confirmed the gate [check: years].
records.inference: Yadin read the three as one royal design, built under Solomon, exactly as 1 Kings 9:15 lists them. This view became the standard one for a generation.
records.limit: The plan alone does not date a gate: six-chambered gates were built at other places and later times. The dating rests on the pottery found with each, and on the strata beneath and above.

records.title: The low chronology
records.evidence: In 1996 Israel Finkelstein proposed in the journal Levant that the pottery style used to date these strata to the 10th century belongs to the 9th, so that the gates and palaces once called Solomon's belong to the Omride kings of the north [check: Levant 28 (1996)].
records.inference: On Finkelstein's view, Jerusalem under David and Solomon was a modest highland town and the large state belongs to the 9th century. He sets this out for a general reader with Neil Asher Silberman in The Bible Unearthed (2001) and David and Solomon (2006).
records.limit: The low chronology is a re-dating of pottery, not a new find. It moves Solomon's buildings, but does not by itself show that Solomon did not build.

records.title: The conventional and modified views
records.evidence: Amihai Mazar proposed a modified conventional chronology, in which the pottery period called Iron IIA spans both the 10th and 9th centuries [check: the range]. William Dever has defended a 10th-century Gezer gate. Steven Ortiz and Samuel Wolff, excavating Gezer from 2006, report 10th-century fortifications there [check: their publications]. Radiocarbon studies have been run by teams on both sides.
records.inference: Radiocarbon has narrowed the gap between the views to decades, though it has not closed it: on many readings the dates fall close to the turn of the 10th to the 9th century, which both sides can claim [check: the summary given in a recent survey].
records.limit: Radiocarbon gives ranges, and a century as short as the tenth is near the edge of its precision. The debate is real and continuing, and this study reports it without choosing a stratum.

records.title: Copper in the south
records.evidence: Erez Ben-Yosef's work at Timna and in the Faynan region has dated large-scale copper production to the 10th century BC [check: publications and range].
records.inference: Ben-Yosef argues that a people who lived largely in tents could still run an organised state with little monumental building, so that a lack of stone buildings is weak evidence against a kingdom. This is his inference, and others have applied it to Edom more than to Israel.
records.limit: The copper is not tied to Solomon by any inscription. It bears on how archaeologists argue from what is missing.

records.title: Shishak, a fixed point
records.evidence: 1 Kings 14:25 says Shishak, king of Egypt, came against Jerusalem in Rehoboam's fifth year, just after Solomon's death. Shoshenq I's list of conquered places on the temple wall at Karnak is usually dated to about 925 BC.
records.inference: Shoshenq's campaign is the nearest outside record to Solomon's reign, and it shows Egypt treating the land as worth a campaign directly after it. Israel among the empires (07) reads the list.
records.limit: The Karnak list's preserved names do not include Jerusalem, and how its route is read is argued. Its date rests on Egyptian chronology, itself a reconstruction.

views.name: Early date, about 1446 BC
views.forIt: The plain sense of 1 Kings 6:1 and Judges 11:26. Wood's dating of Jericho's fall to about 1400 BC, and his placing of Ai at Khirbet el-Maqatir.
views.against: Raamses in Exodus 1:11; the timing of the hill-country villages in the 12th century; Kenyon's and the radiocarbon dating of Jericho.
views.wouldShow: An Egyptian or Canaanite record of the 15th or early 14th century naming Israel, beyond dispute.

views.name: Late date, about 1260 BC
views.forIt: Raamses and Pi-Ramesses; the 13th-century fire at Hazor; the rise of the highland villages; Israel on the Merneptah stele a generation later.
views.against: It reads the 480 years of 1 Kings 6:1 as a measure, not a count, and must account for Jephthah's 300 years and for Jericho and Ai.
views.wouldShow: A city of the 13th century at Jericho or at Ai, or an Egyptian record of the 13th century that names the exodus events.

debates.name: The length of the stay in Egypt

views.name: About 430 years in Egypt
views.held: Readers who follow the Hebrew text's main line, among them Eugene Merrill [check: Merrill's position on the sojourn, in Kingdom of Priests].
views.forIt: The Hebrew wording of Exodus 12:40 and the 400 years of Genesis 15:13.
views.against: The four names of Exodus 6:16–20; Paul's count from the promise in Galatians 3:17.
views.wouldShow: Nothing on the ground can show this; it is a question of the text.

views.name: About 215 years in Egypt
views.held: The Greek and Samaritan texts; Josephus; Seder Olam and Rashi (210 years); some evangelical scholars [check: name one before publishing].
views.forIt: The ancient textual reading; the four generations; Galatians 3:17.
views.against: The Hebrew wording reads more naturally of Egypt alone, and Genesis 15:13 gives 400 years of affliction.
views.wouldShow: As above, the text, not the ground.

views.name: Et-Tell
views.held: Most archaeologists, following the excavations of Marquet-Krause and Callaway.
views.forIt: Its size and its place east of Bethel at Beitin.
views.wouldShow: A Late Bronze occupation not yet found.

views.name: Khirbet el-Maqatir
views.held: Bryant Wood and the Associates for Biblical Research.
views.forIt: A Late Bronze fortress with destruction by fire, and a reading of Joshua 7–8's geography.
views.against: It requires Bethel at Beitin to be read with a nearby Ai of modest size; its dating is published mainly by the excavators.
views.wouldShow: Independent publication and review of the excavated dating.

views.name: Modified conventional
views.note: One pottery period spans the 10th and 9th centuries; Solomon's building can be recognised in it.

views.name: Low chronology
views.note: The gates are 9th-century work; David's and Solomon's Jerusalem was modest.

inventionView.head: Israel's early history as invention: others' view, and the answer
inventionView.theirs: From the 1990s a group of scholars, sometimes called minimalists, argued that the Bible's account of Israel before the kings, and much of the united kingdom, was composed in the Persian or Hellenistic period and tells us more about its writers than about the past. Philip Davies set out the case in In Search of ‘Ancient Israel’ (1992); Thomas L. Thompson in The Mythic Past (1999); Niels Peter Lemche in several works; Keith Whitelam in The Invention of Ancient Israel (1996). In their terms, the biblical Israel is a literary construction, to be kept apart from the historical Israel known from the ground.
inventionView.answer: Evangelical scholars answer on two fronts. On method, Iain Provan, V. Philips Long and Tremper Longman III argue in A Biblical History of Israel (2003; second edition 2015) that ancient texts are testimony, to be weighed rather than set aside until confirmed, and that the silence of the ground is weak evidence. On evidence, Kenneth Kitchen, in On the Reliability of the Old Testament (2003), sets the Bible's details beside the record of their period: Israel on the Merneptah stele, the house of David at Tel Dan, Shoshenq's campaign, and the forms of treaties and lists. Excavations since, among them Khirbet Qeiyafa, have added organised building in the time Samuel describes.
inventionView.beyond: The invention view was also opposed by many archaeologists who are not evangelicals. William Dever, in What Did the Biblical Writers Know and When Did They Know It? (2001), argued strongly against it, while not accepting the whole biblical account. This is reported so that the reader knows the view is a minority one in the field, not to borrow Dever's other conclusions.
inventionView.siteVoice: The site holds Scripture to be truth, without any mixture of error (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article I). It describes the invention view as others' view and does not hold it. What Scripture says of itself is taught in the theology study Scripture (the word of God), not argued here.
inventionView.limit: The ground can show that the people and places of the account fit their world. It cannot prove, by itself, that a particular event happened, and it cannot disprove one by its silence.

claims.head: Silence is not a verdict.
claims.evidence: No Egyptian record names the exodus, under either date. Egypt's surviving records seldom recorded defeats, and people living in tents in Sinai leave little to dig. Israel stands in Canaan on the Merneptah stele by about 1208 BC.
claims.inference: The lack of a record is consistent with the event not having been recorded, or not having survived, as well as with its not having happened. The ground cannot choose among these.
claims.limit: Nor has archaeology proved the exodus. What it can show is a setting: Semites in the Delta, a Raamses, an Israel in Canaan by 1208 BC.

test.question: No Egyptian text from the 13th century mentions the plagues. What follows?

options.why: An absent record is weak evidence where so little survives and defeats were rarely written up.

options.text: The plagues happened in the 15th century instead.
options.why: No 15th-century record mentions them either. The silence does not choose a date.

options.text: The Egyptian record that survives cannot settle the question either way.
options.why: That is what the silence can bear.

claims.claim: “The walls of Jericho have been found fallen flat, proving Joshua.”
claims.head: Fallen walls, yes. Whose date is the question.
claims.evidence: Garstang, Kenyon and Wood all describe collapsed fortifications and a burned city. Kenyon dated the destruction about 1550 BC; Wood about 1400 BC.
claims.inference: On Wood's date the ruins fit the early exodus. On Kenyon's they are too early for either date.
claims.limit: The finding is real; its link to Joshua depends on its date, which is disputed. Cities through their layers (08) reads the layers.

test.question: A website says Jericho's fallen walls prove the Bible. What do you ask first?

options.text: Whose date for the fall it is using, and on what evidence.
options.why: The walls are agreed; the date is not, and the date decides whether they fit.
Every excavator saw them. That is not where the argument lies.
A destruction of 1550 BC and one of 1400 BC say different things about Joshua.

claims.head: His name, a century and a half later. Building, in his time.
claims.evidence: The Tel Dan stele names the house of David in the 9th century BC. Khirbet Qeiyafa shows a planned, fortified town in Judah's lowland around the late 11th or early 10th century. The summit of the City of David holds large building whose date is argued.
claims.inference: A king called David, founder of a line, was known abroad within about a century and a half. There was organised building in his region and time.
claims.limit: No inscription from David's own reign names him. Who built Qeiyafa, and when the Jerusalem building was raised, are argued.

test.question: What does the Tel Dan stele let you say about David?

options.text: That his palace has been found.
options.why: The stele is from Dan, far to the north, and names his house, not his building.

options.text: That a foreign king of the 9th century knew Judah's royal line by David's name.
options.why: That is what the stone carries.

options.text: That his kingdom reached the Euphrates.
options.why: The stele says nothing about the extent of his reign.

claims.claim: “Solomon's three gates prove 1 Kings 9:15.” Or: “Solomon's gates belong to a later king.”
claims.head: One plan, three cities. The date is the argument.
claims.evidence: Six-chambered gates stand at Hazor, Megiddo and Gezer, the three cities 1 Kings 9:15 names. Their dating rests on pottery and, more recently, radiocarbon.
claims.inference: On the conventional view the gates fit the verse closely. On the low chronology they are 9th-century work. Radiocarbon has narrowed the gap to decades without closing it.
claims.limit: Both slogans outrun the evidence. The gates are compatible with the verse; whether they are the very works it names depends on a dating still argued.

test.question: Radiocarbon dates from one gate's layer fall around 950 to 880 BC. What can you say?

options.why: The range runs into the following century, so a later builder is not excluded.
The range includes the years usually given for his reign.

options.text: The range allows either builder, and other evidence must decide.
options.why: That is what a range of this width can carry. The figures in this question are illustrative, not a published result.

confusedWords.word: A date in the text and a date for the text
confusedWords.note: 1 Kings 6:1 gives a date in the story. When Kings was written is another question, handled by How the Old Testament books were written.
The 480 years read as a count of years gives about 1446 BC; read as a measure of generations it gives a later date. Both readings take the verse as true.
A burned layer shows a city fell. It does not show who brought it down.
Nothing of a period found at a site may mean it was never there, that it eroded, or that it lies in an unexcavated part of the mound.
Et-Tell is a site; Ai is a name in Scripture. Joining them is an identification, argued from geography and finds.
There is no pottery that says Israelite. There is pottery of the early Iron Age found where Israel lived, and in other places too.

The low chronology re-dates strata by about a century. Minimalism is a view of the Bible's history as late invention. Finkelstein holds the first and has opposed the second in several respects [check: the wording of his position before stating it on the page].

stance.head: What this site holds
stance.confessionSource: Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article I (the Scriptures)
stance.body: The site holds that the exodus, the entry into the land, the judges and the kingdom of David and Solomon happened as Scripture tells them. Every date on this page is a reconstruction: a joining of the text's numbers to the ground's ranges. Where scholars who hold Scripture true join them differently (the exodus date, the stay in Egypt, Ai, the tenth century), this page shows each view and does not choose. Where a view denies what the text claims, it is described as others' view, with the answer.

reach: Six stations and about twenty sites and records are read here; many other sites of the period are left out, among them Lachish, Arad, Beth-Shemesh and Tel Rehov [check: whether a neighbour study reads any of them].
No excavation report was read in full for this draft. Every attribution of a view to a named scholar is marked for checking against that scholar's own text before the page is built.
Egyptian dates are given on the usual chronology; Egyptologists differ by a decade or more for this period, which moves every fixed point.
Radiocarbon dates are given only as their publishers' ranges, and this page does not recalibrate any of them.
This study reports the archaeology of the sites; it does not read the Hebrew of the passages. How Hebrew works and the theology book studies do.
